paper.title: Taxation and International Migration of Superstars: Evidence from the European Football Market
paper.code_data_availability: The article page carries additional materials and author disclosure statements (http://dx.doi.org/10.1257/aer.103.5.1892), and the reference list includes the AER dataset deposit: …

registers.name_in_paper: full population data from Denmark provided by Statistics Denmark
registers.role: outcomes and sample frame for Figure 4: annual counts of foreign workers resident in Denmark by earnings relative to the tax-scheme eligibility threshold and by industry (sports and entertainment versus all other industries)

registers.name_in_paper: European football data on the universe of first-league players and clubs in 14 countries, collected from online sources (mainly playerhistory.com)
registers.role: treatment assignment (country of location), outcomes (fractions of foreign and domestic players, club performance) and the player quality index

registers.name_in_paper: individual player salary data for about half of the sample, shared by Jori Pinje
registers.role: construction of actual and imputed individual earnings, used to compute average tax rates for 1996-2008

registers.name_in_paper: own top earnings tax rate database (national tax codes; OECD Taxing Wages calculators; UEFA rankings for performance measures)
registers.role: treatment variable: top marginal and average earnings tax rates on domestic and on foreign players, including preferential immigrant schemes

linkages: Players linked across countries and years by name, nationality and date of birth to trace career paths across the 14 first leagues
Players linked to clubs by club affiliation, and clubs to country-level UEFA performance points
Players linked to country x year tax rates by country of location, year and foreign status (plus quality cell for the grouped average tax rate)
Figure 4: foreign workers in Danish full-population data linked to industry classification and to annualized earnings relative to the scheme eligibility threshold

sample.universe: The universe of first-league football players and first-league clubs in 14 European countries since 1985 (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, England, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland); for Figure 4, the full population of foreign workers resident in Denmark 1980-2005
sample.unit_of_observation: player x year (multinomial location choice); country x era averages for the cross-country reduced form; country x year for the synthetic control case studies; industry x earnings-group x year counts for Figure 4
selection_rules: 14 Western European countries, all the top football leagues in Western Europe according to official UEFA rankings; Eastern Europe, Russia, Turkey and Scotland excluded for lack of data before the late 1990s
Players restricted to citizens of one of the 14 countries who have played at least once in a first league of one of these countries
Only year x player observations in which the player was playing in one of the first leagues of the 14 countries are retained
Second leagues of England, France, Germany, Italy and Spain added for robustness; because second-league information is only available since 1999, that analysis is restricted to 1999-2008
Regression analysis focuses primarily on the post-Bosman era 1996-2008; column 7 of Table 2 uses the pre-Bosman era 1985-1995
Figure 4: foreigners in Denmark with annualized earnings above the scheme eligibility threshold (treatment) and between 80 percent and 99.5 percent of it (control)
sample.n_observations: 55,225 player-year observations in Table 2 columns 1-6 (post-Bosman 1996-2008); 45,577 in Table 2 column 7 (pre-Bosman 1985-1995); 47,727 in Table 3 panel A (top leagues 1999-2008); 70,703 in Table 3 panel B (adding the five best second leagues)

construction_notes: The relevant tax rate for the year-t season is the calendar year t tax rate, because the composition of the team for the year-t season is determined mostly before the beginning of the season

The top earnings tax rate combines the top individual income tax rate (national and local), uncapped payroll taxes (employee and employer social security contributions without an earnings ceiling) and value-added taxes
A separate series of top earnings tax rates on foreign players accounts for preferential schemes for immigrant workers (Netherlands 1980s, Denmark 1991, Belgium 2002, Spain 2004, France 2008)

The main analysis assumes equality between the average and the top marginal tax rate; average tax rates are computed from actual and imputed individual earnings with OECD Taxing Wages calculators for 1996-2008 and are averaged by cells of year x country x foreign status x quality (a grouping estimator) to avoid endogeneity
Counterfactual wages are assumed equal to actual wages using PPP exchange rates

The player quality index is built from career outcomes up to year t - 1 only; four dummy variables for the quartiles of the current-year quality distribution are used in the regressions; an alternative index uses the average quality of a player's clubs over the three preceding seasons
In the reduced-form case studies, top-quality players are those selected at least once for the national team of their home country over their career to date; lower-quality players are the rest
Country-level club performance is the total number of points earned by all clubs of a country in UEFA competitions, computed with UEFA's formula

Synthetic control countries are built with nonnegative Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) weights that minimize the pre-reform distance in the outcome and in indexes of football league quality (Spain: 66-88 percent on Italy, plus England, France, Portugal; Denmark: 63-77 percent on Sweden, plus England and especially Norway)
Figure 4 series are normalized to one in 1990, weighted by duration of stay during the year for part-year foreign residents, with earnings annualized for part-year residents

claims.statement: In the pre-Bosman (1985-1995) era, a higher net-of-tax rate for foreign players across countries is associated with a higher the fraction of foreign players in the top league, with an elasticity of 0.00 estimated with respect to the top marginal tax rate.

treatment.label: net-of-tax rate on foreign players, log(1 - tau_f)

definition.value: One minus the average top earnings tax rate for foreign players in the country, assuming eligibility for preferential immigrant tax treatment when applicable; the top earnings tax rate is computed including all taxes on labor income (national and local income taxes, uncapped payroll taxes and VAT); entered in logs

timing.value: Country average of the calendar-year top earnings tax rate over the era (1985-1995 pre-Bosman or 1996-2008 post-Bosman)

outcome.label: log of the fraction of foreign players in the top league of a country

definition.value: The fraction of foreign players of the total number of players playing in the top league of a country, averaged over the era and entered in logs as the dependent variable; only nationals of the 14 sample countries count as players, so the fraction of foreigners excludes nationals from outside this set of countries

timing.value: Country average over the era (1985-1995 pre-Bosman or 1996-2008 post-Bosman)

units.value: elasticity of the fraction of players with respect to the net-of-tax rate (log-log, unitless)

magnitude.interpretation: The elasticity is zero in the pre-Bosman era

estimand.target_population: First-league football players in the 14 sample countries, pre-Bosman (1985-1995)
estimand.time_horizon: Long-run: the regression uses country averages over the whole pre-Bosman era 1985-1995

population.description: The 14 Western European countries whose first leagues are in the sample (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, England, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland), as country-level averages over the pre-Bosman era 1985-1995
population.region: Western Europe: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, England, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland
subgroups_defined: pre-Bosman era 1985-1995
post-Bosman era 1996-2008
foreign players
domestic players
population.selection: Players restricted to citizens of one of the 14 sample countries who have played at least once in a first league of one of these countries; players with multiple nationalities excluded; only year x player observations in which the player was playing in one of the 14 first leagues are retained

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-country variation in top earnings tax rates across the 14 sample countries, contrasted between the pre-Bosman era (1985-1995), when UEFA's three-player and transfer-fee rules restricted mobility, and the post-Bosman era (1996-2008), after the December 1995 Bosman ruling removed them

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-Bosman cross-country correlation between top earnings tax rates and mobility/performance is causal
key_assumptions.supported_by: The pre-Bosman period, when mobility was restricted by UEFA rules, is offered as a successful placebo test

rhs: unobserved country determinants of player location and club performance

key_assumptions.assumption: The Bosman ruling did not have differential impacts on low-tax and high-tax countries for nontax reasons (for example through the correlation of tax levels with country size and league quality)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussed as a threat to identification; no test offered

key_assumptions.assumption: No other factors changed between the pre-Bosman and post-Bosman eras that impacted low-tax and high-tax countries differentially
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussed as a threat to identification; the paper notes the 1985-1990 ban on English clubs and reports that dropping England leaves the estimates virtually unchanged

threats_discussed: The Bosman ruling could have had differential impacts on low-tax and high-tax countries for nontax reasons, e.g. because tax levels correlate with country size and league quality
Other factors could have changed from the pre-Bosman to the post-Bosman era that impacted low-tax and high-tax countries differentially
The 1985-1990 ban on English clubs from international competitions after the Heysel Stadium disaster biases down migration to and from England pre-Bosman
The standard errors are too large to detect a significant difference between the pre-Bosman and post-Bosman estimates
robustness_checks: Average tax rates instead of top marginal tax rates (Table 1, column 2)
Eliminating England from the sample leaves the elasticity estimates virtually unchanged (results not reported)
The pre-Bosman era as a placebo period in which mobility was restricted
Quasi-experimental country case studies (Spain, Denmark) that control for these threats
unresolved_confounders: Correlation of taxation levels with country size and therefore league quality, if better leagues benefited more from the Bosman ruling
Any other pre- to post-Bosman change affecting low-tax and high-tax countries differentially

estimation.specification: Univariate cross-country OLS regression of the log era-average outcome on the log of the net-of-tax rate, one observation per country, estimated on era averages for 1985-1995; no country weights, no controls and no country fixed effects
estimation.weights: None - the regression uses no country weights

source_table.value: Table 1, panel A1, column (1)

heterogeneity.finding: The elasticity of the fraction of foreigners is 0.00 (0.86) pre-Bosman and 1.22 (0.45) post-Bosman; for domestic players it is 0.09 (0.04) pre-Bosman and 0.29 (0.08) post-Bosman. The standard errors are too large to detect a significant difference between eras.

Post-Bosman the elasticity is much larger for foreign players (1.22) than for domestic players (0.29), because the fraction of foreigners is around 10 percent while the fraction playing home is around 85 percent, so the denominators of the two elasticities differ while the slopes are similar.

ambiguities: The paper notes it has much more power for cross-effects of tau_f than of tau_d, so there may be significant displacement effects of domestic players on foreigners that it cannot estimate; the insignificant estimate is therefore recorded as a tested null rather than as a negative effect.

Columns 4 and 5 contain no main log(1 - tau) term, so the interactions with low and top are the level effects of the net-of-tax rate for each quality group rather than deviations from a common effect.

evidence.panel: Panel B. Adding the five best second leagues (1999-2008)

value.lhs: U^i_nt (utility of player i from playing in country n at time t)

value.normalisation: Multinomial logit over the country alternatives; home^i_n is a dummy equal to one if country n is the native country of player i; ability enters as four dummy variables corresponding to each quartile of the quality distribution in the current year, and the quality index for individual i in year t uses only career outcomes up to year t - 1
value.link_function: multinomial logit (type I extreme value distributed error nu^i_nt)

target_designation.reasoning: The Table 3 note designates the quality interactions as the evidence of sorting effects and the foreign/domestic cross-interactions as the displacement effects; both are the coefficients of interest in columns 4 and 5.
